He just sat down on the grass, cross-legged, and waited, making the clicking sound Biscuit liked. After a minute the little dog wriggled back through the gap, muddy to the shoulders, tail going. Fernando scooped him up and held him against his chest, and then, before going in, he wedged a flowerpot into the hole.

I'd been on a work call when I let Juniper out, and an hour later I realized I hadn't heard her come back in. I went to the yard and called her name once, in my ordinary voice, and waited. Nothing. I noticed the old urge to panic start up somewhere behind my ribs, and I noticed it like I'd notice a sound in the next room, without going to it. Juniper is fourteen and nearly deaf. She doesn't run off anymore; she sleeps. So I walked the yard slowly, checking the places an old dog would go: under the porch, behind the rain barrel, in the long grass by the compost. The evening air was cool and smelled of lilac. I found her at last in the far corner under the lilac bush itself, curled in a hollow she'd dug, fast asleep, her side rising and falling. I knelt in the damp grass beside her and put my hand on her ribs and felt her breathing. I didn't wake her. I sat there with her a while as the light went, my hand rising and falling with her breath, until she lifted her head and blinked at me.

When Ravi Shankar noticed the back gate swinging open, he understood why the dog hadn't come in. He set down his mug on the porch rail and took a long breath. His daughter came out, already crying, asking where Mango was. He knelt and held both her hands. "Mango is a smart dog," he said, slowly and clearly. "She knows her name and she knows our street. We'll find her." He gave her a job: stand at the gate and shake the treat bag every minute. Then he walked down the lane with a flashlight, unhurried, calling the dog's name at an even volume, pausing after each call to listen. Porch lights came on. A neighbor in a bathrobe said she'd seen a yellow dog heading toward the park. Ravi thanked her and kept walking. At the park, under the swings, he found Mango rolling in something that smelled terrible, delighted with herself. He clipped on her leash and laughed. On the way back he could hear the treat bag rattling from two houses away, faithfully, every minute, and he slowed his steps to enjoy the sound.

Our dog Pepper is a digger, so when she didn't come in from the yard after breakfast, I had a pretty good idea what she was up to. I put my shoes on, refilled my coffee, and walked out into the cool morning. The grass was soaked with dew and my socks were wet within three steps. I didn't care. I followed the trail of disturbed earth along the fence to the vegetable bed, and there was a Pepper-shaped hole and no Pepper. I sipped my coffee and thought about it. The fence was intact. The gate was latched. That meant she was still here somewhere. I stood very quietly and listened. After a minute I heard a faint scrabbling sound coming from under the old garden shed. I lay down on my stomach in the wet grass, coffee mug set carefully aside, and looked under. Two eyes and a very dirty nose. "Morning," I said. Her tail thumped against the floorboards. I lay there talking to her for a while, the sun warming my back, until she decided on her own to crawl out, and then I hosed us both off.

Old Mrs. Kowalczyk called for Duchess three times from the kitchen door, and when the little terrier didn't come, she put on her coat and her rain boots, took her cane from the hook, and went out to look. It was nearly dark. The garden was long and overgrown at the back, and she walked it slowly, tapping the cane ahead of her to find the path. She was eighty-six and had lost dogs before, not to death, just to rabbits, and they always came home. She hummed under her breath as she went, a song from the radio when she was a girl. At the bottom of the garden, by the compost heap, she stopped and stood still and listened. A faint whine came from inside the hedge. She bent, very slowly, one hand on her knee, and parted the branches with the cane. Duchess was stuck there, her collar caught on a twig, looking very sorry for herself. "Silly girl," Mrs. Kowalczyk murmured, unhooking her with patient fingers. She tucked the dog under one arm and walked back up the path at the same slow pace.

It had been forty minutes and Bruno still hadn't come back inside, which wasn't like him; he's a big lazy mastiff who hates the cold. I went out onto the deck. Snow had started falling, thick flakes drifting down through the porch light, and the yard was already turning white. I stood there a moment and just breathed the cold air and watched them fall. Then I followed his tracks. They were easy to see, big paw prints going in a slow line across the lawn and around the side of the garage. I followed them without hurrying, my slippers soaking through, the snow squeaking softly under my weight. They ended at the side door of the garage, which was open a crack. Inside, on the old couch we'd moved out there last spring, Bruno was lying on his back with his legs in the air, snoring. I laughed so loudly he opened one eye. "Fine," I said. "Stay here." I went back in, got his blanket and mine, and sat with him on that old couch for a while, watching the snow through the dusty window.

From the wings, Oyelaran could see a slice of the audience: rows of faces in the dim light, a man in the front row folding his program into a fan. The stage manager whispered two minutes. Oyelaran rolled his shoulders back, one at a time, and let them drop. He held his cello by the neck and ran his thumb along the smooth, cool wood the way someone might stroke a sleeping cat. He'd played this Bach suite a thousand times, in his bedroom, in subway stations, at his father's funeral. It lived in his hands now more than his head. He closed his eyes and listened to the house: the cough, the shuffle, the low hum of the air conditioning. His breath slowed until he could feel his heartbeat in his fingertips, unhurried and even. The stage manager touched his elbow. He opened his eyes, nodded, and walked out into the light at an ordinary pace, set the endpin, settled the instrument against his chest, and waited until the last rustle in the hall had died away before he lifted the bow.

I always arrive early, so I had a full hour backstage before the set. I spent it doing small things: tuning, then retuning, then wiping the strings down with a soft cloth, then sitting on an equipment case eating an apple and watching the sound tech coil cables in big, neat loops. The opening act was loud and I could feel the bass through the floor, through the case, up my spine. People kept poking their heads in to ask if I was nervous. I told the truth: not really. I'd played smaller rooms that scared me more. This room was big and dark and full of people who had paid to hear music, and that seemed like a kind thing to walk into. When the opener finished, I stood up, stretched my arms over my head until my back popped, and picked up my guitar. My hands were warm and dry. In the corridor to the stage I let my fingers run over the chords of the first song, silently, the way you'd mouth a word before saying it, and then I stepped out onto the stage and said good evening into the microphone.

Liesl Hoffmann sat at the piano bench before anyone else came into the hall, adjusting it a centimeter forward, then back again. The recital wasn't for another forty minutes. The stage lights weren't on yet and the room had the cool, dusty silence of a theater in the afternoon. She placed her hands on her lap and looked at the keys without touching them. She was sixteen and had played in competitions since she was eight, and she'd learned that this moment, alone with the instrument before the room filled, was the one she should take. She breathed into her belly and let the breath go, three times, slowly. Her teacher came in quietly and sat in the last row and didn't say anything, which Liesl was grateful for. She played a single soft scale, C major, just to feel the weight of the keys. Then she stood, smoothed her black dress, and went backstage to wait. When her name was called an hour later, she walked out, bowed, sat, and found the bench exactly where she had left it, just right.

My first open mic. I was third on the list, sitting at a sticky table in the back of a bar with my ukulele across my lap, and the guy before me was so loud and so nervous that he dropped his pick twice. I felt for him. I also noticed that I didn't feel what he was feeling, not even a little. Maybe it was because I'd decided ahead of time that whatever happened would be fine, that I was just there to play two songs for strangers on a Wednesday. My breathing was slow. My fingers rested on the strings without pressing. I watched the bartender polish glasses, holding each one up to the light. When they called my name I walked to the little stool at the front, sat down, and adjusted the mic to my height, taking my time. The room went mostly quiet. Someone's phone buzzed. I smiled out at the dim faces and said, "This one's about my grandmother's kitchen," and started to play, and my voice came out exactly the way it does in my own living room.

The choir lined up in the corridor behind the church in their navy robes, forty of them shuffling and whispering, and Abuela Consuelo stood at the very end of the line where the altos always went. She was seventy-nine and had sung in this choir for fifty years. A young soprano near the front was trembling, her music folder shaking in her hands. Consuelo walked up the line, put her own warm hand over the girl's, and held it there. "Look at me, mija," she said quietly. "Breathe with me." They breathed together, in through the nose, out through the mouth, slow as a tide. The girl's shoulders came down. Consuelo smiled and patted her cheek. "You know this song in your bones. Let your bones sing it." Then she went back to her place at the end of the line, folded her hands on her folder, and closed her eyes. Through the door she could hear the organ beginning the prelude, the deep notes humming in the floor under her feet. When the line began to move, she moved with it, step by measured step, into the candlelit church.

They told me I'd be going on in five minutes, and I nodded and went back to sitting on the floor of the green room with my back against the wall and my violin case open beside me. I'd been there for twenty minutes and I liked it there: the hum of the mini-fridge, the bad carpet, the faint sound of applause for the act before me coming through two closed doors. I lifted the violin out and held it under my chin without playing, just to feel it settle in that familiar place against my jaw. It always feels like coming home. I plucked the A string and listened to it ring all the way down to nothing. My hands were steady. I noticed my heartbeat and it was slow, maybe a little slower than usual, which happens to me before shows; I seem to go quiet inside while everyone else goes loud. A volunteer stuck her head in. "You're up." I stood, smoothed my shirt, and walked down the corridor behind her, rolling my bow arm in small loops, and stepped out into the warm light.

The box on the doorstep was addressed to Henrik Aalto in careful block capitals, with no return address. He carried it inside and set it on the kitchen table, then made his coffee first, because the coffee was already brewing and the box was not going anywhere. He sat down across from it with the mug and studied it as he drank. A Finnish postmark. Tape wound around it far more times than necessary. He smiled a little at that; only one person he knew taped things like that. When the coffee was half gone he slit the tape with a butter knife, unhurried, and folded back the flaps. Inside, wrapped in a wool sweater, was a jar of cloudberry jam and a note from his aunt in Oulu: Saw these and thought of your summers here. Henrik held the jar up to the window and watched the light glow orange through it. He set it on the counter where he would see it every morning. Then he unfolded the sweater, held it to his face for a moment, smelled woodsmoke and cedar, and pulled it on over his shirt.

A package showed up that I definitely hadn't ordered: a long, flat box, heavier than it looked. I checked the label twice. My name, my address. No sender. I put it on the floor of the living room and sat cross-legged in front of it, and I noticed I was curious rather than wary, the way you'd be curious about a shell on a beach. I opened it slowly, peeling the tape back in one strip. Inside was bubble wrap, and inside the bubble wrap was a framed print of a painting I'd admired at a gallery months ago, a gray sea with one red boat on it. I'd mentioned it to exactly one person. I sat back on my heels and laughed softly, and then I just looked at it for a long time. The red boat. The gray, gray water. I didn't text her right away. I wanted to sit with it a little first, alone. I found a nail in the junk drawer, chose a spot on the wall where the afternoon light would fall, and hung it carefully. Then I sat on the couch and looked at it while the light shifted.

Mariam Al-Sayed had just come in from the garden, soil on her knees, when the courier handed her a box the size of a microwave. She hadn't ordered anything. She set it on the porch step, washed her hands under the outdoor tap, and dried them on her trousers before she touched it again. The return address was a seed company. She frowned slightly, puzzled but not troubled, and opened it on the step with her pruning knife. It was full of bulbs, dozens of them, tulips and alliums and some she didn't recognize, with a packing slip made out to the previous owner of the house, a Mrs. Hollis, who had moved to a care home in the spring. Mariam sat on the step with a bulb in her palm, turning it over. Mrs. Hollis had planted the garden Mariam loved so much. She looked out at the beds, at the bare patches by the fence where tulips must once have stood. Then she found a pencil and wrote a note on the packing slip: Your bulbs went in on Saturday. I will send photos in April. She started digging that afternoon.

The package was small and heavy and covered in stamps from Chile, and I didn't know anyone in Chile. I turned it over in my hands on the walk up the stairs, feeling the weight shift inside. In the kitchen I set it on the counter and looked at it while I put away my groceries, one thing at a time, eggs, milk, the bag of lemons. There was no urgency to it. Whatever it was, it would still be there in five minutes. When the groceries were away I opened it with scissors. Inside, wrapped in newspaper, was a smooth black stone the size of a fist and a postcard: Found this on the beach where you told me your father used to fish. Thought it should go home with you. M. It took me a moment. Matías, the backpacker I'd shared a train compartment with two years ago and talked to all night. I held the stone and it was cool and solid and fit my palm exactly. I put it on the windowsill above the sink, where I wash dishes every evening and look out.

Grace Achterberg opened the unexpected package on her lap in the armchair by the radiator, a crocheted blanket over her knees. She was ninety-one and didn't get many parcels anymore. She took her time with the string, working the knot loose with her thumbnail rather than cutting it, because the string was good string and she'd keep it. Inside, under tissue paper, was a photo album she had never seen. Her great-grandson had scanned and printed every photo from her old shoebox, the one in the closet, and arranged them in order: her wedding, the farm, the flood year, the children as babies. Grace turned the pages slowly, one at a time, resting her hand flat on each before she turned it. She didn't cry. She hummed. She knew every face. On the last page was a note in a boy's handwriting: For Oma, so they don't fade. She closed the album and held it on her lap with both hands, and sat looking out the window at the bare birch in the yard, rocking slightly, until the nurse came in with tea.

I came home to a package leaning against my door, soggy from the rain, with my name smeared but readable. No idea what it was. I brought it in and set it on a towel on the floor, then changed into dry clothes and made myself a toasted cheese sandwich before going back to it. There's something nice about not rushing a surprise. The cardboard was so wet it practically opened itself. Inside was a ceramic mug, slightly lopsided, glazed a deep green, and a note from my niece: I made this in pottery class!!! It's for your tea!!! It leaks a tiny bit at the handle!!! I laughed out loud alone in my apartment. I filled the kettle. While it heated I held the mug, turning it in my hands, feeling the thumbprint she had left by accident near the rim. I fit my own thumb into it. When the water boiled I made tea in it, and it did leak a tiny bit at the handle, a slow bead running down to the saucer. I sat by the window with it and watched the rain until the tea was gone.

Joaquín and his sister Carmela had been at it for three hours, and the grandmother's apartment was starting to look like someone else's: boxes, bags, bare walls with pale rectangles where photographs had hung. Carmela kept stopping to cry, and each time Joaquín set down what he was holding and waited beside her until she was ready to go on. He was in no hurry. Neither of them had to be anywhere. When she pulled out Abuela's sewing tin, the old blue cookie tin full of buttons, she laughed through the tears. "She used to let us sort these." Joaquín sat down on the floor and held out his hands, and Carmela poured half the buttons into them. They sorted them the way they used to, by color, on the rug, into little piles. Red, brown, mother-of-pearl. The afternoon sun came through the lace curtains and made patterns on their hands. Neither of them spoke for a long time. When they were done, Joaquín poured all the buttons back into the tin together and handed it to his sister. "You keep it," he said. "I'll come over and sort them."

My brother wanted to rush, and I understood that. He had a flight on Sunday and a lot of feelings he didn't know what to do with. I didn't want to rush. So I took the kitchen and gave him the closets, and I worked slowly through Nana's cupboards, one shelf at a time. Her chipped teacups. A tin of loose Darjeeling, still fragrant when I lifted the lid. Spices in old jam jars with handwritten labels: cardamom, hing, fennel. I smelled each one. I could hear him in the bedroom, the scrape of hangers, a sudden silence. I went to the doorway and found him sitting on her bed holding the green shawl she wore every winter. I sat beside him and didn't say anything. The mattress sagged and tipped us toward each other. After a while I took the shawl gently from his hands and folded it, edge to edge, in quarters, the way she always did, and laid it in his lap. "Take that home with you," I said. He nodded. We sat there until the light went orange, and then I made us tea from her tin.

The three Macleod sisters had agreed that whoever found something and wanted it would just say so, and that there would be no arguing. It was Fiona, the youngest, who kept them to it. When Moira and Kirsty both reached for Gran's silver brooch at the same moment and their voices began to sharpen, Fiona put down the tablecloth she was folding and came over. "Let's sit," she said, and they did, on the edge of the old four-poster bed. Fiona held the brooch up to the window. It was shaped like a thistle with an amethyst in the center. "Remember she wore it to every christening?" Moira said. "And to bingo," Kirsty said, and they all laughed. Fiona waited, turning it slowly in the light. Her voice, when she spoke again, was soft and unhurried. "What if it goes to whoever has the next baby christened? And then gets passed on?" Her sisters looked at each other. Kirsty, who was six months along and not yet showing, went pink. Fiona smiled, pressed the brooch into her palm, and went back to folding the tablecloth.

We found her recipe cards in a shoebox at the back of the pantry, held together with a rubber band that snapped when my sister touched it. Hundreds of them. We sat on the kitchen floor, the two of us, our backs against the cupboards, and went through them one by one. My sister read each title out loud and I'd say whether I remembered it. Lamingtons, yes. Pumpkin scones, yes. Mutton curry, God, yes, every Sunday. Some had notes in the margins in Gran's spidery hand: too much salt, Reg didn't like, good for church. I didn't feel heavy, which surprised me. I felt the opposite, like sitting by a window in the sun. The kitchen smelled faintly of her still, of eucalyptus soap and burnt sugar. My sister laughed at one that just said Biscuits I Made Up and had no instructions at all. We decided to split them evenly and then, a minute later, decided not to. We'd photocopy them and each keep a set. I put the box under my arm, and we went out to the back step and sat in the late sun a while longer.

Samisoni and his older brother Viliami had not spoken much in the last few years, and nobody expected them to sort their grandmother's things together without a quarrel. But Samisoni had decided on the drive over that he would go slowly, and he did. He let Viliami choose first in every room. When his brother reached for the woven mat that hung above the couch, the one their grandmother had made as a girl in Tonga, Samisoni felt a small pang, because he'd wanted it too. He noticed the feeling, let it pass, and said nothing but "Good, she'd want that." Viliami looked at him strangely. Later, in the kitchen, Samisoni found her old wooden kava bowl and ran his palms over the smooth worn rim. Viliami came and stood beside him. "You take this," his brother said, roughly. "You were the one who sat with her and drank with the uncles." Samisoni nodded. They stood side by side at her window, looking out at the frangipani tree she had planted, its white flowers scattered on the grass, and for a while neither of them said anything, and it was fine.

My cousins were arguing in the next room over who would get the piano. I stayed where I was, in Babcia's bedroom, sitting on the floor in front of her dresser with the bottom drawer open. It was full of letters and holy cards and ribbon. I took each thing out and looked at it and put it in a pile, slowly, the way you'd turn pages of a book you weren't trying to finish. The raised voices came through the wall and I let them. They weren't mine to fix right now. I found a little paper bag with a lock of baby hair in it, labeled with my mother's name in pencil. I held it in my palm for a long moment. My breath was slow and deep and I could smell the lavender sachets she'd tucked into every drawer. When the shouting stopped, my youngest cousin wandered in looking wrung out, and sat down next to me without a word. I handed her a stack of holy cards. She started looking through them too. After a while she leaned her head against my shoulder, and I kept going through the drawer with one hand.

Mohan Pillai unlocked the hardware store at seven fifty-five, five minutes before opening, the way he had every Monday for twenty-six years. He switched on the lights in sections, front to back, and listened to each bank of fluorescent tubes flicker and hum to life. The store smelled of machine oil and sawdust and the faint sweetness of the birdseed by the door. He put the cash float in the till, counting it twice out of habit, coin by coin, enjoying the cool weight of each roll. Then he took the broom from behind the counter and swept the front step, though it didn't really need it. A bus went by. A man on a bicycle nodded to him and Mohan nodded back. He turned the sign on the door from CLOSED to OPEN and propped the door with the iron doorstop shaped like a dog. Then he went back behind the counter, poured himself a cup of tea from his flask, opened the newspaper to the crossword, and waited, without any urgency, for whatever the week would bring through the door.

I own a little bookshop and Monday mornings are my favorite hour of the week. Nobody comes in until ten. I let myself in at eight with my key and a pastry from the cafe on the corner, and I don't turn on the overhead lights, just the lamps, so the shop glows like the inside of a lantern. I put the kettle on in the back. While it heats, I walk the shelves with my coffee and straighten things that got pushed around over the weekend: a poetry book in the cookery section, a children's book face down on the floor. I don't rush any of it. I read a page here and there. The radiators tick as they warm up. Outside the window, people hurry past to the train with their collars up, and I watch them with a kind of tenderness. When the kettle whistles I make a pot and set it on the counter by the register, with a stack of mismatched cups, for anyone who might come in. Then I sit on my stool, open the box of new arrivals, and cut the tape with a single slow stroke of the knife.

When Leilani Kahale arrived at her flower shop on Monday, the refrigeration unit had died over the weekend and half the roses were wilted in their buckets. She stood in the doorway for a long moment, her keys still in her hand, looking at them. Then she set down her bag, propped the door open to let in the cool morning air, and began. She lifted each bucket out of the warm cooler one at a time and carried it to the shady back room. She sorted the flowers quietly, stem by stem: these could be saved, these could not. She recut the good ones at an angle under running water, her fingers wet and cold. A delivery driver came in and whistled at the mess. "Rough start," he said. "Could be worse," Leilani said, smiling, and offered him a sprig of eucalyptus for his dashboard. She called the repair company and was put on hold, and hummed along with the hold music while she kept cutting. By nine, the shop smelled green and fresh, and a bucket of half-price roses sat on the sidewalk with a handwritten sign: A little tired, still lovely.

Monday at the bakery starts at four in the morning, and I like it best before anybody else arrives. The streets are dark and empty. I unlock the back door, flick on the ovens, and let the room fill with that dry, rising heat. The dough I left to proof on Sunday afternoon is waiting under its cloths, puffed and soft, and when I press a finger into it the dent fills back slowly, which means it's right. I tie my apron. I scale the loaves on the old brass scale my father used, one by one, and shape them on the floured bench, folding, turning, tucking, a motion my hands know better than my mind does. The radio is on low, a farming report, prices for barley. There's nothing to think about but the dough. By six, the first loaves are out, crackling as they cool on the racks, and the whole street smells of crust. I unlock the front door, flip the sign, and stand in the doorway for a minute with my arms crossed, watching the sky go from navy to gray, waiting for the first regular.

Signora Bellini had run the little grocery on the Via Garibaldi for forty years, and on Monday mornings she opened it the same way every time. First the shutter, which she rolled up with a long hooked pole, letting it rattle up into its housing. Then the crates of fruit on the pavement, arranged by color: lemons, oranges, then the dark plums. She took her time placing each piece, turning the best faces outward. A neighbor's child stopped on the way to school and she gave her an apricot, as she did most mornings. Inside, she wiped the counter with a damp cloth in slow circles and set out the scale. She switched on the small radio by the register to the station that played old songs and sang along under her breath, a little flat. A delivery van double-parked outside and the driver hollered for her signature. She signed with a flourish and sent him off with a peach. Then she pulled her stool to the open doorway, sat with her hands folded on her apron, and watched the street come awake, nodding to each person who passed.

The Monday after the robbery, Tuan Nguyen opened his phone repair shop exactly as he always did. Someone had broken the front window on Saturday night and taken a few cheap chargers; the glass had been replaced on Sunday, and the new pane was very clean, cleaner than the rest of the shop. He stood outside and looked at it for a moment, his hands in his jacket pockets. His wife had wanted him to stay home today. He had thanked her and come in anyway. He unlocked the door, turned on the lights, and swept up the last tiny glints of glass from the corner the workmen had missed. He refilled the display of chargers. He wiped the counter. When his first customer came in, an elderly woman with a cracked screen, she noticed the new window and asked what happened. He told her plainly, without heat, and she clucked her tongue. "It's only things," Tuan said, shrugging, and took her phone gently in both hands. She watched him work, his fingers steady as he opened the case with a small blue tool, and by the time he finished she was telling him about her grandchildren.

The line at the food bank was already around the block when Beatriz Navarro arrived at seven, and the delivery truck was late. Other volunteers were checking their phones and muttering. Beatriz tied on her apron and walked outside to the line. She went person to person, slowly, introducing herself, saying the food would be a little late but that it was coming and everyone would get a box. She crouched to talk to a little boy holding his mother's hand and asked him what his favorite cereal was. He told her, very seriously, that it was the one with the marshmallows. She promised to look for it. Back inside, she organized the other volunteers into an assembly line with a few soft words and a lot of pointing, and when the truck finally rumbled up she was first to the back of it, lifting boxes and passing them along in a steady rhythm, never faster than she could keep up. At the end of the day she found one box of marshmallow cereal in the dry goods, and she set it aside, and she waited by the door until the boy came through.

My job at the food bank is the produce table, and I like it more than I expected to. Someone hands me crates of whatever came in, cabbages, apples, a mountain of slightly soft tomatoes, and I sort them, pile them, and help people choose. It's slow work. You pick up each tomato and check it with your thumb. You set the bruised ones aside for the soup kitchen next door. You chat. A man in a painter's overalls comes every Saturday and always asks if there are any onions, and today there were, and his whole face changed. I gave him an extra one without saying anything. The hall is noisy with voices, carts squeaking, kids running in the aisles, but at my table it always feels oddly hushed, like the eye of something. My hands smell of earth and celery by noon. When a young mother apologized for taking so long to choose, I told her honestly that there was no hurry, and I stood beside her while she picked, holding the bag open, until she'd found the six best apples in the crate.

Abdirahman Farah had volunteered at the food bank every Thursday since he retired from driving buses, and the newer volunteers had learned to watch how he did things. He never hurried. When a woman came to the counter flustered, digging through her purse for a form she'd forgotten, Abdirahman leaned on the counter and waited, smiling, and then told her softly that it was fine, they'd do it next week. When the pallet jack jammed, he knelt beside it and looked at it for a long while before he moved anything, and then he fixed it with one firm push. When a teenage volunteer dropped an entire case of canned beans and stood frozen among the rolling cans, he simply began picking them up, one by one, humming, until she joined him. At the end of the shift he swept the warehouse floor in long strokes from one wall to the other. Then he sat on an overturned crate by the loading dock, drank a cup of the bad coffee from the urn, and watched the sun set over the parking lot, his hands resting easy on his knees.

It was my first shift at the food bank, and the coordinator handed me a clipboard and put me on intake. I'd expected to feel out of my depth, but the feeling never came. There was a simple rhythm to it: smile, ask their name, check the list, hand them a number. A woman in a nursing uniform. A grandfather with three small grandkids. A college student who wouldn't meet my eyes. I tried to give each of them the same unhurried attention, looking up from the clipboard, saying their name back to them. The student finally glanced up when I did that, and gave me a small nod. My voice stayed low and even all morning. At one point the printer broke and the line backed up, and people started shifting their weight and sighing. I stood up and told them what was going on and that I'd write the numbers by hand. Then I did, carefully, on index cards. Nobody left. By the end of the shift my hand ached from writing, and I felt as if I'd slept for ten hours.

Sister Philomena ran the Saturday pantry out of the church basement, and she had a gift for slowing a room down. When she came down the stairs at nine, the volunteers were shouting over each other about where the donated turkeys should go. She stood at the bottom step, one hand on the rail, and said nothing at all until they noticed her. Then, quietly: "Good morning. Shall we start with the turkeys?" They followed her to the big chest freezer. She had them stack the turkeys one at a time, counting out loud together, and the counting itself seemed to settle everyone. By ten the doors were open and the line came in out of the cold. Philomena stood at the end of the tables and greeted each family by name. She remembered whose son had the flu, whose daughter had just started kindergarten. A man came in late, ashamed, after everything was handed out. She took his arm, walked him back to the storeroom, and found him a turkey that had been set aside, she said, specifically for whoever arrived last.

The first hour at the food bank I sorted donations, and that's when I found out how much I like doing simple things with my hands. Someone dumps a big bin of mixed groceries on the table and you sort it: cans with cans, pasta with pasta, check every date, set aside anything expired. Peanut butter. Soup. A lone jar of capers, which made me smile; somebody cleaned out a fancy pantry. I lined everything up in neat rows by size. My breathing got slow without my trying. The music from someone's speaker was old soul, and the woman next to me, a retired librarian named Delphine, sang along under her breath. We didn't talk much. We didn't have to. Every now and then she'd slide a can over to me without looking, because it belonged in my row, and I'd do the same for her. By lunchtime we'd cleared six bins. My back was stiff and my fingers were dusty and I felt more settled than I had in weeks. She bumped her shoulder against mine on the way out. "Same time next week?" I said yes before she finished asking.

The waiting room at St. Columba's had orange plastic chairs and a television bolted to the wall playing a cooking show with the sound off. Edwin Marsh sat in the corner with his hat on his knee, waiting while his wife was in surgery. It was a routine operation, the surgeon had said, two or three hours. Edwin had brought a book and hadn't opened it. He found that he didn't want to read. He wanted to watch the room. A young couple across from him held hands and stared at the floor. A teenage boy was playing a game on his phone with the volume very low. A janitor mopped the far end of the corridor in long, overlapping arcs, and Edwin watched the shine spread across the tiles. He breathed slowly. He thought of his wife's face this morning, joking with the nurse about the gown. Every so often he turned the brim of his hat a little in his hands. When the young woman across from him began to cry quietly, he got up, fetched a cup of water from the cooler, set it on the chair beside her, and went back to his seat.

My father was in the ER with chest pains and they'd told me to wait. So I waited. The chairs were hard and the lights hummed and a man two rows ahead of me was arguing with the front desk in a voice that kept rising. I noticed my own breathing, and it was slow, and I decided to keep it that way. I'd been through this before with Dad. Getting worked up wouldn't make the doctors any faster. I took off my jacket and folded it on the seat beside me. I bought a packet of crackers from the vending machine and ate them one at a time. I texted my brother: Here, waiting, will update, no news yet. Then I put my phone away and looked out the window at the parking lot, where an ambulance sat with its back doors open and two paramedics were laughing at something. I watched a sparrow pick at crumbs under a bench. When a nurse finally came out and said my name, I stood up, picked up my jacket, and walked over to her without hurrying, ready to hear whatever she had to say.

Svetlana had sat in this waiting room every Tuesday for six weeks while her mother had chemotherapy, and by now she had her rituals. She took the chair by the fish tank. She brought her knitting, a long red scarf that had grown about a foot each week. She bought a weak coffee from the machine and let it go cold beside her, because she didn't really want it; she just liked holding it at first. The fish moved through the water in slow loops, a striped one always hiding behind the plastic castle. Svetlana counted stitches under her breath, purl, knit, purl, and the click of her needles fell into a soft rhythm with the bubbling of the tank. The receptionist knew her name now and waved. An old man she often saw nodded at her from across the room and she nodded back. They had never spoken. They didn't need to. When the oncology nurse came to the door at half past three and smiled at her, Svetlana finished her row, tucked the needles into the yarn, and stood, stretching her back before going in.

My wife was in labor, and the nurses had sent me out while they did a procedure, so I was sitting in the waiting area at two in the morning in a paper gown over my clothes. It was quiet. A vending machine glowed blue in the corner. One other man was asleep across three chairs with his coat over his face, snoring gently. I had expected to be pacing. Instead I sat with my elbows on my knees and my hands loose between them, and I felt very still and very awake, like the moment before a wave lifts you. I looked at my hands. They were steady. They would be holding someone soon. I thought about that for a long time. I listened to the faint sounds from down the hall: a door, a voice, a beep. At some point the sleeping man woke up, sat up, rubbed his face, and looked over at me. "First one?" he said. I nodded. He smiled and lay back down. "You'll be fine," he said into his coat. I believed him. I leaned my head back against the wall and waited for them to call me back in.

Kamala Iyer had driven her neighbor to the hospital when his hand got caught in the lawnmower, and now she sat in the emergency waiting room with his wallet and keys on her lap. He'd gone through the swinging doors forty minutes ago, wrapped in a dish towel, gray in the face but joking. Kamala had worked thirty years as a school nurse and knew what the doctors would do and roughly how long it would take. She folded her hands over his wallet. The room was crowded: a child with a fever, a young man holding an ice pack to his eye, a woman with her arm in a makeshift sling. Kamala noticed the child's mother looking frantically around for something, and leaned over and offered her a tissue from her handbag. The mother took it gratefully. They talked a little, about fevers, about how children bounce back. Kamala's voice was low and warm and she asked simple questions. The mother's shoulders came down from around her ears. When the doors swung open and her neighbor came out with his hand bandaged in white, Kamala stood, smiled, and held out his keys.

They'd taken my son back for an X-ray after he fell off the climbing frame, and I wasn't allowed to go with him, so I sat in the waiting room holding his stuffed rabbit. It's a gray rabbit with one ear chewed thin. I held it on my knee and smoothed the chewed ear between my thumb and finger, over and over. The waiting room smelled of disinfectant and the cheap coffee someone had spilled near the door. A toddler was drawing on the whiteboard in the corner with intense concentration. A man was reading a newspaper, turning the pages with a loud rustle. I let my eyes rest on all of it, not looking for anything. My son had been crying when they wheeled him in, but he'd also been asking whether he'd get a cast in a cool color, which seemed like a good sign. I found myself smiling at that. My breath went in and out, long and slow. When the door opened and a nurse waved me over, saying he was asking for the rabbit, I stood up, tucked it under my arm, and went to find him.
